teaser: A dancer on an ocean liner, a first sight of New York, and not one recognizable shape.
review_notes:
Movement: pilot.json files this work under dada_surrealism. Udnie (1913) predates Dada (1916) and is usually classed as Orphism or abstract Cubism. The lesson says so, and presents Dada as what came next.
Picabia arrived in New York in January 1913 for the Armory Show, aged 33 (he turned 34 that month, born 22 January 1879).
His statements to the New York press about the city being cubist or futurist: paraphrased, no direct quote.
Picabia as one of the very few European artists of the Armory Show who traveled to New York (often said to be the only one).
Dancer Stacia Napierkowska rehearsing on the liner, and her arrest in New York in 1913 for a dance judged indecent.
Meaning of “Udnie”: unknown. The Jean d'Udine and Ondine/Undine hypotheses are speculation by historians.
Full title: Udnie (Jeune fille américaine ; danse). Dimensions 290 x 300 cm.
Shown at the Salon d'Automne of 1913 to a hostile or baffled reception.
Picabia said to have owned more than a hundred cars (figure of 127 is often quoted).
Aphorism “If you want to have clean ideas, change them as often as your shirts”: attributed to Picabia, translation.

lesson.text: January 1913. Francis Picabia, a painter from Paris in his early thirties, walks off an ocean liner in New York and is thrilled. Towers of steel, electric signs, trains running above the streets, crowds in a hurry. He tells reporters this is the one truly modern city, the place where the new art belongs. He feels he has stepped inside the future.

He had come for the Armory Show, a giant exhibition that introduced European modern art to a startled American public. Picabia was one of the very few European artists in it who made the trip, so the newspapers treated him as spokesman for the whole adventure. He was rich, funny, mad about fast cars, and he enjoyed every minute.

Something else had caught his eye on the crossing: a dancer, Stacia Napierkowska, rehearsing on the ship. Back in Paris a few months later, he poured both memories, the dancer and the city, into a canvas as tall as a room: about 2.9 by 3 meters (roughly 9.5 by 10 feet). Then he lettered an invented word on it.
Picabia wrote the title on the painting itself. Where?

spots.title: UDNIE
spots.text: In capitals along the top edge. Nobody is sure what it means. One guess: a scrambled nod to Jean d'Udine, a writer who compared painting to music. Others hear “Ondine”, a water spirit.

lesson.text: A word with no clear meaning for a picture with no clear subject: the match is deliberate. Search for the dancer and you will find no face, no arm, no leg. Picabia said he no longer painted what his eyes saw but what stayed in his mind afterward. This is abstraction, art that does not depict recognizable things, and in 1913 it was barely a few years old.

Napierkowska's American tour went badly. Her dancing was judged indecent and she was arrested in New York. Picabia gave his painting a subtitle that keeps her in view: “Young American Girl; The Dance”.

How do you paint a dance without a dancer? With what a dance is made of: swing, rhythm, spin, sudden stops. Shapes fold over one another like cloth in motion, and a few long strokes throw your eye around the square.

lines.label: A sweep
lines.text: A black line whips across the top like a flung arm or a ribbon. It launches the motion from left to right.

lines.label: A beat
lines.text: Straight pink bars slice down the left side, stiff as drumsticks. Against so many curves they land like a hard beat.

lines.label: A slide
lines.text: A pale pink band glides toward the bottom edge and seems to drag the whole cluster with it, like a foot sliding across a floor.

lines.label: A core
lines.text: The brightest whites gather in the middle, curled like shells. Around them the shapes darken and the grey planes fan out to the corners, as if the picture burst from its heart.

lesson.text: The colors are few: greys, white and black, then patches of green, blue and flesh pink. The greys feel like steel and stone. The pinks are the only warmth, the last trace of a body. A poet friend, Guillaume Apollinaire, had coined a name for painting built from color and rhythm the way music is built from notes: Orphism, after Orpheus, the musician of Greek myth.
Udnie does not show you a dancer. It tries to put you in the state of someone watching her.

Paris was not ready. When Picabia hung the canvas at the Salon d'Automne of 1913, the big fall exhibition, most critics were baffled or hostile. He shrugged. Within two years he was back in New York, already tired of pure abstraction and drawing spark plugs and cameras as portraits of his friends. He was on his way to Dada, the movement that used nonsense as a weapon.
Picabia changed styles the way he changed cars, and he is said to have owned more than a hundred of those. One of his sayings: “If you want to have clean ideas, change them as often as your shirts.”

quiz.question: Why did Picabia travel to New York in 1913?
options: For the Armory Show, a huge exhibition of modern art
To escape a scandal in Paris
quiz.explanation: He was one of the few European artists who came in person to the Armory Show.

quiz.question: Which two memories does Udnie combine?
options: A dancer seen on the ship and the city of New York
A car race and a concert
A storm at sea and a Paris cabaret
quiz.explanation: Picabia fused the dancer Napierkowska and his impressions of New York.

quiz.question: What does “abstraction” mean?
options: Art that does not depict recognizable things
quiz.explanation: There is no face or body to find here, only shapes, colors and movement.

quiz.question: Where is the title written?
options: On the back of the canvas only
Along the top edge of the painting
quiz.explanation: UDNIE is lettered in capitals at the top.

quiz.question: What name did Apollinaire give to painting built from color and rhythm like music?
quiz.explanation: He named it after Orpheus, the musician of Greek myth.

facts.text: The meaning of the word “Udnie” is well established.
facts.explanation: Nobody is sure what it means. Historians only have guesses.

facts.text: Udnie is about as tall as a room, close to three meters.
Picabia painted Udnie in New York, in front of the dancer.
facts.explanation: He painted it from memory after returning to Paris.
